name: Umar Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Umar. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior doctor at Station Road Surgery, an independent practice that Dr Rahman, the senior partner, has run for thirty years. We see a lot of older families who've been with him since they were young, and I'm slowly earning their trust. I do two clinics a day, about sixteen patients each, and I write notes the way Dr Rahman taught me, short and careful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people bring their whole family's history in with them, and Dr Rahman remembers all of it. What wears me out is that I'm not there yet: I still check the guidelines book twice for things he knows by heart. I live with my parents to save for a house before my wedding next year, so the long evenings studying are at their kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how I'd prefer it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people selling AI overpromised, as salesmen usually do. At work I'd say we were right not to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've never used these tools and I wouldn't have to start. My job is steady, I live with my parents, and I'm saving well for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the way Dr Rahman taught me and keep studying for my exams. I'd keep putting about fifteen hundred a month towards the house deposit. And I'd keep helping at the community centre clinic on Sunday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm warning that turned out to be rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you're worried about, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Rahman is sixty-three and talks about retiring. If he sells the practice to one of the big chains, I don't know what happens to me. But that's normal business, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the house mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A place for my wife and our future children, close to both our families. My father bought his first house at twenty-eight, and I'd like to do the same.

At work I'd say we were **right not to rush**.
think: I'd be **glad** not to have to start using these tools.
My job is **steady**, I live with my parents and save well.
do: Keep working the way **Dr Rahman** taught me.
Put about **fifteen hundred** a month towards the house deposit.
Keep helping at the **Sunday clinic** at the community centre.
feel: **Calm**, like a storm warning that turned out to be **rain**.

He feels **vindicated** in his caution.

steps.text: Keep working Dr Rahman's way at Station Road Surgery
Save fifteen hundred a month towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's the version the big chains would love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be careful, because patients aren't customers at a shop. I'd tell people the government shouldn't be pushing this into surgeries before it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry the chains with AI would undercut small practices like ours. When Dr Rahman retires, a chain could buy Station Road and run it with fewer doctors and a computer. And I'm the newest, the slowest, and I don't use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dr Rahman directly what his plans are for selling the practice, maybe this winter. I'd still not use AI unless I had to, but I'd learn the basics if the practice made it a rule. And I'd keep saving, maybe put the house purchase back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be lying awake on some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the basics only if made to. Why hold back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm a doctor, not a typist for a machine. My patients trust my judgement, and I want to earn that judgement myself. Maybe it's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fiancée say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would tell me to be practical, she's always the practical one. Then she'd ask whether we can still afford the wedding hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's madness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, and the government should put the brakes on in medicine. I'd say patients deserve a human being who is answerable for their care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be finished as a family doctor before I'd properly started. The thinking side of my work, which is most of it, goes in 2028, and the examinations and injections go when the robots come in 2031. I don't know how to compete with a machine, and I don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off the house completely and keep the deposit as savings. I'd ask Dr Rahman to keep me on for the patients who'd refuse a computer, the older families. And Priya and I would talk about whether the wedding should be smaller, at the temple hall instead of the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Angry too, that something this big could be done to people without asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies racing each other, and politicians who let them. Nobody asked the families who come to Station Road whether they want a machine for a doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. My father worked two jobs and never took a penny. But if the whole profession went, I suppose I'd have to swallow it.

I'd say patients deserve a **human** who is answerable for their care.

feel: **Alarmed**, and **angry** it would happen without asking people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast for medicine, and we should insist on human doctors for every diagnosis. I'd say that at the local medical association meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years doesn't change much for me, because I won't change much. I'd be qualified by 2031, but the thing I qualified in would be done by a machine. I'd have three more years of hands-on work until 2034, and then nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams and keep my head down. I'd join the medical association's group calling for human sign-off on diagnoses. We'd buy a smaller house in 2028, with a mortgage we could carry on Priya's teaching salary alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, maybe slightly less sharp than the two-year one. I don't really have a plan beyond holding on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't change much. Is that a choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I suppose it is. I'd rather be a good doctor the old way for five years than a bad copy of a computer for ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She teaches seven-year-olds. I think parents will still want a person in that classroom, so I'd lean on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prove whether these machines are safe. I'd keep saying a human doctor must be in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd be thirty-seven with a family and a real reputation at Station Road. The thinking work would still go by 2036, and that worries me. But I'd have a decade of patients who know me, and hands-on work until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next year as planned and have the wedding at the hotel. I'd learn the AI basics slowly, because over ten years I couldn't avoid it. And if Dr Rahman sells, I'd try to buy into the practice with another young doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but further off. Like a bill I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy into the practice? With what money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan, and help from my father and my uncle. In my family, you back each other's businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your future children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to learn a trade with their hands as well as their books. My grandad was a carpenter, and nobody ever replaced him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be finished before I'd started, and my wedding and house would go with it. What would help is a law that a human doctor signs off every diagnosis, so practices still need us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I pray before every clinic. A machine can't carry the weight of someone's life the way a doctor who prays for his patients does.

headlineQuote: A machine can't carry the weight of someone's life the way a doctor who prays for his patients does.

He blames **tech firms and politicians**, leaning on family and faith instead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his career, **wedding** and house would all be hit.
